notes: The first signal surfaced by the new ecological_early_warning lane. Threatens SI1 (acute stress on freshwater ecosystems, fish and habitats from record-low flows) and SI4 (reduced dilution concentrates pollutants and worsens measured water quality); informs the SI8 baseline as a climate-change hazard materialising, the pressure the resilience indicator is about. The horizon point is structural, not seasonal: 2022 was the first official Welsh drought since 2005/06, and 2025 and 2026 have followed, so three declared droughts in five years read as a recurrent climate-driven pressure on the freshwater and climate-resilience indicators, which a policy-worded scan would never have caught. Cited to the Welsh Government Written Statement (external to NRW) rather than NRW own pages. The flow specifics and the 190-year figure are carried by NRW's Dry Weather Blog 2026 (the cited Welsh Government Written Statement covers the declaration and areas); the July record is described as a projection (on course for), not a confirmed figure.
summary: On 23 July 2026 Natural Resources Wales declared drought status for Gwynedd, Ynys Mon, Clwyd, the Dee and the Upper Severn, with South and West Wales moving to prolonged dry weather. A Welsh Government Written Statement the same day confirms exceptionally low flows on the Clwyd, Dyfi, Alyn, Clywedog, Conwy and Tanat, with new record minimum flows on the Clwyd and the Erch, alongside wildfires and successive heatwaves. North Wales and the Upper Severn had under 2 percent of expected July rainfall, on course for the driest July in almost 190 years.
title: NRW declares drought status for North Wales as July 2026 nears a 190-year rainfall low
